title: Advanced Model Binding Concepts in ASP.NET Core
description: Master binding source attributes (FromForm, FromBody, FromQuery, FromRoute, FromHeader) and collections binding.

data.text: Introduction to Model Binding Sources

ASP.NET Core's model binding automatically maps incoming HTTP request data to action method parameters. By default it searches form data, then route values, then query strings — in that order. But you can explicitly control where data is bound from using binding source attributes.

terms.definition: The automatic process of mapping HTTP request data to action method parameters.
An attribute like [FromForm] or [FromQuery] that tells model binding exactly which source to read from.
Key-value pairs sent in the body of an HTTP POST request.
Key-value pairs appended to a URL after the ? character.
Values extracted from the URL route pattern, such as {controller}, {action}, {id}.

data.caption: How ASP.NET Core model binding searches for values across different request sources.

data.text: Binding Source Attributes Overview
ASP.NET Core provides five binding source attributes. Each one locks model binding to a single source, overriding the default search order.

data.title: Why use binding source attributes?
data.text: Without a binding source attribute, model binding searches all three default sources in order. Using an attribute makes your intent explicit, avoids ambiguity, and can improve security by preventing over-posting.
The [FromForm] Attribute

The [FromForm] attribute tells model binding to get values exclusively from the HTTP request's form data. Since form data is already the first place model binding looks, this attribute is often optional for standard form posts — but it makes your intent clear and is required when the same action can receive data from multiple sources.

The [FromBody] Attribute

The [FromBody] attribute instructs model binding to read the entire request body. This is the standard approach for RESTful API endpoints that accept JSON or XML payloads. ASP.NET Core uses the configured input formatter (e.g., System.Text.Json) to deserialize the body into your model type.

data.title: API Controller — FromBody Example
[FromBody] reads the whole body
data.text: Only one parameter per action can use [FromBody]. The formatter reads the entire request stream, so you cannot combine multiple [FromBody] parameters in a single action method.
The [FromQuery] Attribute

The [FromQuery] attribute forces model binding to look only in the query string. This is useful for GET requests, filter parameters, and search endpoints where data is passed via the URL rather than the body.

data.title: Using [FromQuery] to Override Default Behavior

data.text: In the example above, if the URL is /Products/Search/1?term=laptop, the route value 1 is ignored for the id parameter because [FromQuery] tells model binding to look only in the query string. Since the query string has no id key, id receives its default value of 0.
The [FromRoute] Attribute

The [FromRoute] attribute binds a parameter from the URL route values. This is the default behavior for parameters whose names match route template placeholders, but using the attribute makes the binding source explicit and self-documenting.

data.title: Using [FromRoute] for Explicit Route Binding

data.text: Visiting /products/5 will bind the value 5 from the route into the id parameter. This pattern is central to RESTful API design.
The [FromHeader] Attribute
The [FromHeader] attribute binds a parameter from an HTTP request header. This is useful for reading custom headers like authorization tokens, API keys, or content negotiation preferences.

data.title: Reading a Custom Header with [FromHeader]

data.text: The Name property on [FromHeader] maps the parameter to a header whose name may differ from the parameter name. Without Name, it maps to a header with the same name as the parameter.
Binding All Request Headers with a Model
You can bind multiple headers at once by decorating a model's properties with [FromHeader]. ASP.NET Core will populate each property from the corresponding request header.

data.title: Binding Source Attributes at a Glance

cards.title: [FromForm]
cards.description: Reads values from posted form fields in the request body.
cons: Not suitable for JSON API bodies

cards.title: [FromBody]
cards.description: Reads the entire request body and deserializes it into the model.
cons: Only one parameter per action can use it

cards.title: [FromQuery]
cards.description: Reads values from the URL query string (?key=value).

cards.title: [FromRoute]
cards.description: Reads values from the URL route template placeholders.

cards.title: [FromHeader]
cards.description: Reads values from HTTP request headers.

data.text: Exercise: Try It Yourself

data.title: Build an API Endpoint with [FromBody]
data.description: Create a minimal API or controller endpoint that accepts a JSON payload with a product name and price. Use [FromBody] to bind the JSON to a Product model. Verify it works by sending a POST request with a JSON body.
steps: Create a Product class with Name (string) and Price (decimal) properties.
Add a ProductsController with a POST action using [FromBody] Product.
Return the received product as Ok(product) if ModelState is valid.
Test with a tool like curl, Postman, or the built-in .NET HTTP client.
data.expectedOutcome: A POST request with a JSON body returns the product data. Invalid JSON returns a 400 Bad Request.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Model binding automatically searches form data, then route values, then query strings.
[FromForm] binds from POST form fields; it is the default for HTML form posts.
[FromBody] binds from the request body — use it for JSON API endpoints.
[FromQuery] binds from the URL query string — ideal for GET filters.
[FromRoute] binds from URL route placeholders — essential for RESTful design.
[FromHeader] binds from HTTP headers — useful for auth tokens and metadata.
Only one parameter per action can use [FromBody] because the body stream can only be read once.
data.takeaway: Choosing the right binding source attribute makes your API self-documenting and prevents unexpected binding behavior.
